c39_0.text: Whilst the leadership in the two system elements was acknowledged to be enabling, in the traditional element the managers there were often controlling and restrictive. They appeared to be concerned, worried even about the risks to loosing control, rather than seeing the opportunity to align system ambitions.

c39_1.text: In the two system elements the leaders were seen as being accessible and engaging, whereas in the traditional element they were seen as aloof and inaccessible. Not part of the wider group, distant.

c39_2.text: In the traditional elements leadership was seen less as a process and much more as an asset of individuals, as a privilege that people didn't want to loose, not something to be shared. It was seen as a right that had been acquired. Alternatively, in the system leadership element it was seen very differently, as creating a social leadership movement, investing in the social leadership capital for the benefit of the system over years to come. Totally different perspectives and behaviours.

c39_3.text: I think the distinction between old power and new power Helen Bevan at NHSE works to differentiate between these two traditional elements and the third, the system element. In the system element we can see new power in action, distributed, power though working with and for others, collectively, whereas old power reflects the approach nof managers in the traditional elements, whereby they are in many ways heroic leaders, pacesetting behaviour.

c39_4.text: I would contrast the command and control style leadership behaviours in F with the supportive, consensus building and advocacy type behaviours in B and C.

c39_5.text: In elements A and C leaders seemed to recognise that real power in system situations is collective and doesn't align with status, titles or the number of direct reports you have. They were almost status agnostic, but E I would say that the behaviours of managers and leaders was very much reflective of their status and positional power.

c39_6.text: KPI's, targets and performance measures were used often as stick to beat people with, and I suppose for leaders to hide behind in the two traditional elements that you have selected. This was not the case in element B where leaders were driven and motivated to create a platform for collective success.

c39_7.text: Whilst I wouldn't say that the managers in elements E and F were unambitious, they were much more conservative than the leaders in C who were ambitions to create positive change, improvement, transformation, digitisation etc.

c39_8.text: The outlook of the leaders in elements A and B was strategic and transformational. For element D we have seen a more transactional leadership model, focusing on smaller transactional changes rather than seeing the bigger system picture. Easier to control.

c39_9.text: The managers in elements D and E were driven byn the burning platform right infront of them. They didn't have a longer-term view.

c39_10.text: I would call out that the leadership agenda in elements E and F is much narrower and restricted than in C. In E and F it has felt like managers hide behind structure and governance, as a way of excusing the narrow focus. Also static the agenda isn't emergent at all, nor dynamic, which is the case in C, whereby system leaders have recognised the need for flexibility and the opportunity to be emergent in the way they work with people and communities across the system.

c39_11.text: The depth of the engagement activity in D and F has been superficial, with little weight placed on system relationships, all the attention is placed on immediate and long standing relationships which are safer, unlikely to take different views. No real investment in system thinking.

c40_0.text: In the first two the leaders had direct control, line management responsibility and accountability for the people they were leading. But in the third they didn't. So it was system leadership, leading without direct control or line management responsibility, no positional authority.

c40_1.text: They kind of developed collective direction with the group, whereas in the other two the direction was definitely dictated, people were told how things were going to be.

c40_2.text: Leaders in F were very much rules driven, they were most comfortable when following set rules from the regional and national teams, this meant very little discretion or judgement. Whereas in A and C leaders were more actively explorative, based on the view that new ways to address system issues would only come from thinking more widely than they had previously, taking wider views and engaging a much wider audience to help.

c40_3.text: Leaders views regarding the importance of system relationships differentiates between B and C where relationships were seen as the foundations of system working, but F was different because in this situations relationships were much less important than pace and action which were the priority. Relationships were not seen as a necessary condition for success, more of a nice to have.

c40_4.text: The leaders recognised the necessity for building trust in the system. System leaders saw how important it was to gain, build and foster trust, so this was a real clear objective. Trust was absent in the different situation, here it was all about leaders being directive, lots of go and do, rather than discuss, consider together and think collectively like in the similar ones. The traditional leader was very directive, this is what we are doing so crack on.

c40_5.text: System leaders recognised that nothing can be done quickly from a system perspective because they had to get the collective engaged and understand where there is alignment, as well as where there is tensions or conflict. Need to understand everyone's starting position and their red lines and need to be adaptive. But in the other the focus was short term and the pressure was on short term deliverables.

c40_6.text: Systems leaders were flexible and agile in the way they operated. So they listened and were prepared to flex based on feedback. The others were ridgid in their style and didn't recognise the need for adaptability and flexing, as far as they were concerned they are the leaders so its others that need to adapt to their way of thinking.

c40_7.text: In the third situation that was different the leaders were obsessed with implementing national guidance prescriptively. In the two similar system leadership situations leaders demonstrated their ability to think transformationally, out side of the box, using the collective thinking, power and creativity of the group.

c40_8.text: The leaders played the role of facilitating collaboration between system partners, different organisations coming together, different leaders from different parts of the system. Absolutely collaborative. But in the alternative one leaders acted individually for individual reasons and single motives, not system focused at all.

c40_9.text: There was an over reliance on position power to make things happen at pace. On the other had in B and C the leaders harnessed the social power of the group really effectively, which was much more effective. They recognised that the social power from strong relationships and good engagement was critical to addressing these truly wicked system issues.

c40_10.text: The third was different in that here leaders were supporting people to engage, in the first two they were driving people to deliver. They let the group set its own agenda, gave autonomy and freedom to act.

c40_11.text: The leaders in these two situations brought people together to share learning and they absolutely listened actively to encourage learning reflective learning. This can be contracts against the delivery focus of the leaders in F.

c40_12.text: I would say reflective learning was a big thing in A and B whereas in D it was lla bout the doing and the process, leaders were heavily processual, focus on implementing the process to get things done, disproportionate weight and importance was placed on process.

c40_13.text: In the first two individual participants were set individual goals, and objectives, this was divisive and undermined people working together collectively. In the third there were no individual objectives all objectives were for the group which meant the only way to success was by the collective succeeding which is absolutely in line with system thinking.

c40_14.text: The leadership behaviour in both of the traditional situations could be described as decisive and in some instances even controlling. In contrast, in the system example the leadership behaviours were more about engaging, involving and enabling the system actors to work together, in many ways for the first time in years to work through the big intractable problems.

c40_15.text: Big difference between leaders giving autonomy to the groups in B and restricting autonomy in favour of centralised control in D and E.

c40_16.text: Leaders in C openly welcomed curiosity, but in E and F the focus was on compliance and avoiding grey areas wherever possible.

c40_17.text: A big difference between the first two which were similar and the third which was different was how leaders dealt with mistakes, in the first two mistakes were not acceptable at all. In fact leaders treated people quite harshly when mistakes were made, mistakes had to be avoided, they represented waste in terms of time, resources and energy. However, in the third mistakes were viewed positively as part of the engagement process and more importantly as part of the process of learning, improving,

c40_18.text: The system leaders in A and C were much more visible highly visible in fact, more so than in E where the leaders were much more behind the scenes giving orders. In A and C they were visible working within and as part of the group, because leadership was distributed so they didn't have privileged roles, there were flat structures and shared responsibilities.

c40_19.text: There was a real commitment to co-creation, organic co-creation throughout, across the different groups, which then came together pooled ideas, thoughts, tested ideas, solutions etc. This engagement and collective design approach was seen as important and wholly necessary. Whereas in the other two situations the drive was almost exclusively on implementation, there were clear time pressures and political pressures from the regional and national teams to implement.

c40_20.text: In the system situations there was a lack of clarity, which wasn't helpful, whilst the engagement was positive, there was at times a real lack of clarity as to where we were trying to get to, so lacking clarity of task, intended outcomes and timescales. Almost too much freedom to act, too much decision by committee. There was a need for more leadership direction. However in the two traditional situations there was complete clarity, but in many ways this was too restrictive, no freedom to act.

c40_21.text: In both of the traditional situations the leaders were determined to identify simple almost transactional solutions, they were ignoring the complexity and wickedness of the situations that they were facing, these were system leadership situations but leaders didn't recognise this or may be more accurately they didn't want to recognise this.

c40_22.text: Leadership in B and C emphasised mutuality, system benefits as the driver, but in E leaders were certainly driven by their own vested interests, this was really apparent.

c40_23.text: When I say inclusive I am not talking about diversity I mean the first two were inclusive of all system partners, from all sectors in the system. But the third only included the inner circle, the chosen few, mainly those who would agree, very much like creating an echo chamber.

c41_0.text: In the first two A and C there was shared decision-making, whereas in D it was single leader who took the majority of the decision making alone, in a silo a vacuum. There was too much possession, so everything every result, every decision revolved around a single leader.

c41_1.text: E and F were similar in that both were lead by management thinking, traditional management thinking, which cantered on retaining control and authority and fairly safe decisions. But in C it was very different in so much as the approach of leaders was led by system thinking which recognised that single leaders cannot fix system issues ultimately, it requires collective effort and true collaboration.

c41_2.text: B and C focused on addressing real system challenges, real life wicked issues. Whereas in F the focus was on implementing technical approaches to problem solving. The role of leadership as a social process was minimised completely, technical expertise was deemed to be more relevant and necessary.

c41_3.text: So it was completely different to the system leadership examples, it was completely restrictive, the answer was always no. Even though it made sense, it was always no, there was no feedback as to why either. The other situations were much more permissive, ask for forgiveness not permission. System leadership behaviours were in play, they granted autonomy and distributed accountability, leadership ultimately.

c41_4.text: There was lots of silo working in E and F, leaders and others doing their own thing, little connectivity, and almost no collective or collaborative behaviours, esp at leader levels. In C we say collaborative working between system leaders, using working groups involving multiple system stakeholder reps, feeding back and promoting collaborative actions through joint task and finish groups.

c41_5.text: There was a notable similarity and difference in the way that ownership of issues and problems was perceived by leaders. In D and F individuals were burdened by problems being seen as theirs to solve as individuals. Leaders had the view that it is your problem to solve, its your job, so sort it out. This placed lost of pressure on people, especially as these challenges needed a collective brain they were bigger and messier than leaders recognised, given the system context. They were routine day

c41_6.text: It was very difficult for people to speak up and contribute. There was open and obvious resistance. Whereas in the other one if you challenged that was great, welcomed and facilitated. I'd say the leaders were very open, open to challenge and the benefits fo challenge. So if you disagreed people would normally keep themselves quiet, whereas in the other one the opposite was true. Actually because of this i would also say it was less fun, people didn't want to get involved either.

c41_7.text: In the system leadership situations the leaders harnessed the collective power of the collective, they utilised the scale of multiple inputs, and didn't seek to hold onto knowledge, in fact knowledge was shared for the wider benefit of system partners.

c41_8.text: In B and C leadership was distributed across system partners, intentionally and purposefully to enhance engagement and participation. But very different in D where leadership was held tight and centralised, not shared and certainly not distributed.

c41_9.text: Whilst we saw quite directive leadership in F, a clear and unequivocal leadership directive and mandate which needed to be carried out, we say leader encouraging group think, group direction and group determining its own mandate in A and B. The group experienced group coaching and self reflective practice, there was little leadership, direction.

c41_10.text: This work was the first time the local, regional and national teams had worked together, this was a real crossing of boundaries for us all, but was based on strong principles of collaboration and system working.

c41_11.text: I would say on the right hand side the leadership behaviours were emotionally draining. Lots of pressure, with very little support and almost zero collaboration, very individualised. Really exhausting for individuals. Whereas I think people felt emotionally excited in the other two, there was support, active and dynamic engagement.

c41_12.text: I would say that there was tradition leadership top down decision making in the first two, whereby decisions were hierarchically determined, only made by senior people, leaders and mangers, but in the third the difference was that decisions were taken at all levels and by system partners in all parts of the system.

c41_13.text: The objectives in E and F were very much individual objectives, not shared and without a focus on team achievement. But in B there were no individual objectives, all objectives were set collectively, they were shared. Which meant that everyone was jointly focused on the collective success of the group.

c41_14.text: We built trusting relationships from day one. This meant that we trusted each other and had each others backs. People were trusted to do what they could do and to use their skills to the best effect. It was respectful and trusting, a warm and enabling trusting environment.

c41_15.text: It was hierarchical. You couldn't make decisions or even do anything without going through the hierarchy and getting sign off and approval. No autonomy just hierarchy and overly focused on beaurocracy.

c41_16.text: Establishing respect between all parties was really important in the left hand two, so this was reinforced by leaders at all opportunities, there was a recognition that trust can only be built on mutual respect and this is a foundation for system leadership to work. But this wasn't a priority in the other, in fact there was a lack of mutual respect and this worsened throughout the work.

c41_17.text: Unlike B where everyone had equal standing, all views were valid, welcome and recognised, E and F here the leaders were status orientated, you were recognised based on your pay grade, which either enabled you access to or prevented you from fully participating as equals. The more senior you were the more you had a say and were listened to. That's the way it was.

c41_18.text: In E and F power was through authority, simply through leaders having authority and control. But in B leaders didn't focus on power, they roll-modelled system leadership behaviours, including giving away power and sharing responsibilities as widely as possible with partners and stakeholders and interest groups.

c41_19.text: The system leaders were cult5urally attuned and aware, there is a strong cultural component to system leadership, engaging communities and populations. This is really important to engaging whole systems, to improve things. So here we saw a real emphasis on engaging all parts of the community, and ensuring representation through this engagement. But in the other situation this wasn't seen as important for leaders.

c41_20.text: It could be said that the right hand ones were essentially short-term tactical issues and the leadership was equally short term in its thinking and vision. This was different to C which was strategic, the leaders were thinking and taking actions that would have long term impacts, strategic.

c41_21.text: The leadership in A and C was people cantered and focused very much on building long term and long lasting system relationships. People, relationships were prime, unlike in F where process was prime, it was prioritised over people, seen as necessary for keeping everyone safe. It was actually a major weakness. In A and C people trump the processes but in F the process trumps people. Highly infuriating. Ultimately on this basis the process is the single point of failure.

c41_22.text: There were examples of heroic leadership in the situations on the right hand side, where the leaders set the pace and expected everyone else to keep up with them. There was a lot of ego here, which was a barrier to effective system working. By sharp contrast on the left side A was different this was enabling leadership, where the leaders saw their role as enabling others, creating the right conditions for the wider group to succeed, they weren't looking for lime light and glory themselves. They

c41_23.text: I would contrast controlling leadership behaviours in D and E with much more facilitative leadership in C, which was all about getting the best from the collective capacity, as opposed to controlling the group and exerting power over the end out come.

c41_24.text: In E and F everyone knew that the final destination point had been stitched up, pre-determined by the few senior people. So any engagement was futile and really just for show, because the cards were already marked and the dye had been set. In C the outcomes were genuinely fluid and could be changed and shaped by the group.

c41_25.text: We saw autocratic leadership style in both D and E, not listening and not letting others have their say. In C there was a kind of democracy, everyone had the right to speak up and have their say, they could and were expected to influence.

c41_26.text: And I would say on the right side the leadership is very very risk averse, whereas on the left side we were open to taking a few risks as a system as a collective.

c41_27.text: The name of the game in B and C was engagement and more engagement. This was key to success, at first it didn't actually pay off but then over time system partners really got on board, because of the leadership investment in engagement and not taking the easy option of jumping straight into action.
